title: What a grid convergence study is actually telling you
subtitle: RAE 2822 supercritical section · OpenFOAM rhoSimpleFoam · M∞ 0.729, α 2.31°, Re 6.49×10⁶
thesis: The mesh refinement study did not converge, and saying so is the result — a 23% uncertainty band honestly reported is worth more than a tidy number that is wrong.

paragraphs: The RAE 2822 at M∞ = 0.729 and α = 2.31° is one of the most heavily documented transonic test cases in existence, which makes it a poor place to claim novelty and an excellent place to be rigorous. The aim here was a grid-independent baseline, parametric sweeps in incidence and Mach number, and a turbulence-model comparison — the ordinary verification work that has to sit underneath any result anyone else is going to rely on.
The interesting outcome was not the baseline. It was that the grid study refused to behave, and following that honestly says more about the case than a clean number would have.

blocks.text: Four meshes, and no asymptotic range

paragraphs: Four refinement levels were built with snappyHexMesh, from 24,103 cells to 2,218,368, with mesh quality checked at each level — maximum non-orthogonality stayed between 56° and 61°, average non-orthogonality improved steadily from 9.4° to 5.1°, and no level failed OpenFOAM's own checks. On that evidence the meshes are sound. The forces they produce are not well behaved.

blocks.caption: Lift coefficient against representative cell size across four refinement levels. A converging series should approach a limit monotonically; this one overshoots at the second level and comes back down.

blocks.title: The grid study does not support a tight uncertainty bound
blocks.body: Richardson extrapolation on the finest three levels returns an apparent order of 1.81 for lift and a grid convergence index of 23%. The asymptotic ratio — which should sit near 1 if the series is in the asymptotic range — comes out at 0.127. Drag is worse: non-monotonic across the series, apparent order 0.70, GCI 42%. These are not discretisation-error estimates. They are a statement that the solution is not yet grid converged at 2.2M cells.

paragraphs: There is a plausible physical reason, and it matters because it changes what should be done about it. Extended convergence monitoring at the baseline condition showed the flow sitting close to shock buffet — the forces do not settle to a fixed point so much as hover. If part of what the refinement study is measuring is genuine unsteadiness rather than discretisation error, then no amount of further refinement will produce a clean Richardson fit, because the quantity being extrapolated does not have a steady value to converge to.

The second contributor is more mundane. Average y⁺ on the finest mesh is 108, with a maximum of 383. That is squarely wall-function territory, not a resolved viscous sublayer. For a case whose defining feature is a shock interacting with a boundary layer, near-wall treatment is not a detail — and refining the far field while leaving the first cell in the log layer will not fix the forces.

blocks.text: Turbulence model choice is a result, not a formality

paragraphs: Three RANS closures were run on the identical finest mesh at identical conditions: k-ω SST, k-ε and Spalart-Allmaras. All three agree qualitatively about where the shock sits and how it behaves. They disagree about lift by about 8%.

That spread is larger than most of the effects a parametric study of this kind is used to detect. It means any downstream use of these numbers has to name the closure it came from, and it means a lift value quoted without one is not a measurement of the aerofoil — it is a measurement of the aerofoil and the model together. None of the three reached the residual target within the 2000-iteration budget, which bounds how hard the comparison can be pushed.

blocks.caption: Forces at M∞ = 0.729, α = 2.31° on the 2.22M-cell mesh. Same geometry, same mesh, same conditions.

blocks.text: Where steady RANS answers, and where it only appears to

paragraphs: The incidence sweep from −2° to 6° and the Mach sweep from 0.50 to 0.80 both behave as a supercritical section should: lift rising roughly linearly, drag climbing sharply as the shock strengthens past the design Mach number. Drag at α = 6° reaches 0.087, more than four times the baseline value, and the Mach sweep shows drag divergence setting in between M = 0.75 and M = 0.80.

Two of those points are not really steady. At α = 6° and at M = 0.80 the solution exhibits shock-buffet unsteadiness, and a steady RANS solver asked for a point value under those conditions will return one regardless. The number it returns is an artefact of stopping, not a property of the flow. Both conditions are flagged rather than quoted.

A time-accurate solve with rhoCentralFoam was run from an impulsive freestream to capture shock formation directly. It produced a physically credible development and a drag trajectory consistent with the steady result, then diverged at t ≈ 32 ms with the Courant number reaching about 3.0. Drag had effectively settled; lift and moment had not. It is reported as a qualitative result on a coarser mesh, which is what it is.

blocks.title: What this study supports
blocks.body: A well-resolved qualitative picture of transonic shock behaviour on the RAE 2822, a demonstrated drag-divergence trend, and a quantified sensitivity to turbulence closure. What it does not support is a tight quantitative uncertainty bound on lift or drag, or point values at the two buffet conditions. Both statements are useful; only one of them is comfortable.

paragraphs: Refinement targeted at the near-wall region to bring y⁺ toward 1, rather than uniform refinement of the whole domain — the current series spends most of its cells where they change the answer least. Grid independence re-established at each sweep condition rather than inherited from the baseline. And URANS or scale-resolving treatment for the two buffet points, since no steady method will produce a defensible value there.

Until those are done, this is a verification study that reports an honest 23% rather than a tidy 2%. That is the less impressive-looking result and the more useful one, and it is the same lesson as the transonic solver study: a method is worth exactly as much as your knowledge of where it stops working.
